```{r}
library(sp)
library(maps)
library(sf)
library(lattice)
library(tidyverse)
library(geoR)
library(gstat)
library(INLA)
```


Loading data

```{r}
data(meuse)
data(meuse.grid)
```


Model to build:

$$Y(s) = X(s)'\beta + \epsilon(s)$$
$$\epsilon(s) \sim \textrm{Gaussian Process}$$ 
Spatial Covariance Structures to consider:

Exponential: 
$$\textrm{Cov}\{\epsilon(s), \epsilon(s+h)\} = \sigma^2 e^{- |h / \phi|} $$

Gaussian:

$$\textrm{Cov}\{\epsilon(s), \epsilon(s+h)\} = \sigma^2 exp{- |h / \phi |^2}$$

Spherical:
$$
\textrm{Cov}\{\epsilon(s), \epsilon(s+h)\} = 
\begin{cases}
  \sigma^2(1-\frac{3}{2}|h/ \phi| + \frac{1}{2}|h / \phi|^3) & \text{if } h \leq \phi, \\
  0 & \text{if } h > \phi
\end{cases}
$$


# Data visualization

```{r}
# configuring meuse dataset
coordinates(meuse) <- ~ x + y
proj4string(meuse) <- CRS("epsg:28992")

# configure meuse grid dataset (has distance from meuse river pre-calculated for each location)
data(meuse.grid)
coordinates(meuse.grid) <- ~ x + y
proj4string(meuse.grid) <- CRS("epsg:28992")
gridded(meuse.grid) <- TRUE
```


```{r}
meuse.grid.poly <- as(meuse.grid, "SpatialPolygons") # making meuse.grid belong to the SpatialPolygons class
meuse.bdy <- surveillance::unionSpatialPolygons(meuse.grid.poly)
plot(meuse.bdy)
plot(meuse, add = TRUE, pch = 1)
```

```{r}
# plotting distance to river
spplot(meuse, "dist.m", do.log = FALSE, colorkey = TRUE)

# plotting lead concentration
spplot(meuse, "lead", do.log = TRUE, colorkey = FALSE)

bubble(meuse, "lead", do.log = TRUE, key.space = "bottom")
```

Clearly lead concentration is higher near the river. What will that graph look like when we remove the main effect of distance to river?

```{r}
lead.lm <- lm(log(lead) ~ sqrt(dist), data = meuse)
summary(lead.lm) # dist to river is significant as expected

meuse$fitted.lead = predict(lead.lm, data = meuse)
meuse$fitted.lead = meuse$fitted.lead - mean(meuse$fitted.lead)

meuse$resid.lead = residuals(lead.lm)

spplot(meuse, c("fitted.lead", "resid.lead"))
```

After removing the main effect of distance to river, there is still some inherent spatial pattern occuring in the residuals...

Since these residuals are clearly not independent, we must fit a covariogram function to model them accurately. The three types of covariograms 
underconsideration are the exponential, gaussian, and spherical covariograms.


# Covariograms

Defining some functions for each of the three previously mentioned variograms

All functions take arguments in the order theta = (sigma2, phi, tau) where sigma2 is the overall variance, phi is the range (spatial dependence) parameter, tau2 is the nugget effect

```{r}
# exponential semivariogram
exponential_vario.f <- function(theta) {
  sigma2 <- theta[1]
  phi <- theta[2]
  tau2 <- theta[3]

  function(h) {
    ifelse(
      h == 0,
      0,
      tau2 + sigma2 * (1 - exp(-h / phi))
    )
  }
}

# gaussian semivariogram
gaussian_vario.f <- function(theta) {
  sigma2 <- theta[1]
  phi <- theta[2]
  tau2 <- theta[3]

  function(h) {
    ifelse(
      h == 0,
      0,
      tau2 + sigma2 * (1 - exp(-(h / phi)^2))
    )
  }
}


# spherical semivariogram
spherical_vario.f <- function(theta) {
  sigma2 <- theta[1]
  phi <- theta[2]
  tau2 <- theta[3]

  function(h) {
    ifelse(
      h == 0,
      0,
      ifelse(
        h <= phi,
        tau2 + sigma2 * (
          3 * h / (2 * phi) -
          h^3 / (2 * phi^3)
        ),
        tau2 + sigma2
      )
    )
  }
}
```


Empirical semivariogram

```{r}
meuse_geodat <- as.geodata(
  data.frame(
    coords = coordinates(meuse),
    data = resid(lead.lm)
  )
)

empirical_variog <- variog(meuse_geodat, max.dist = 1500, estimator.type = 'classical')

plot(empirical_variog, main = "Semivariogram")

# checking for presence of anisotropy
plot(variogram(lead ~ dist, data=meuse, alpha=c(0,45,90,135)))  # looks good enough
```


Eyeballing exponential variogram to data:

```{r}
sigma2 = 0.2
tau2 = 0.1
phi = 1000

h <- seq(0, 4500, length.out = 100)

theta = c(sigma2, phi, tau2)

gamma_h <- exponential_vario.f(theta)(h)

plot(empirical_variog$u, empirical_variog$v,
     type = "p",
     pch = 19,
     xlab = "Distance (h)",
     ylab = expression(gamma(h)),
     ylim = range(c(empirical_variog$v, gamma_h)),
     main = "Empirical vs. Exponential Semivariogram")
lines(h, gamma_h, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
legend(
  "bottomright",
  legend = c("Empirical", "Exponential"),
  col = c("black", "blue"),
  pch = c(19, NA),
  lty = c(NA, 1),
  lwd = c(NA, 2)
)
```



Fitting variograms to the data

Maximum likelihood will be utilized to fit our variograms. Other common methods include OLS or WLS, but by using ML we have access to AIC, which is helpful in model selection.

WLS is also a good choice though, since we would like to give points shorter distances away more weight than points farther away.

AIC exp: 171.1
AIC gaus: 170.9
AIC sph: 169

AIC shows no strong preference for any of the models. Technically using the rule of 2, it shows slight prefererence of the spherical variogram.


```{r}
exponential_vario_ML <- likfit(meuse_geodat, cov.model = "exponential",
       ini = c(0.2, 900), nug = 0.1, lik.met = "ML", fix.nugget = FALSE)

gaussian_vario_ML <- likfit(meuse_geodat, cov.model = "gaussian", 
                            ini = c(0.2, 900), nug = 0.1, lik.met = "ML", fix.nugget = FALSE)

spherical_vario_ML <- likfit(meuse_geodat, cov.model = "spherical",
                             ini = c(0.2, 900), nug = 0.1, lik.met = "ML", fix.nugget = FALSE)

# comparing AIC values and looking at param values (sigma2, phi, nugget)
summary(exponential_vario_ML)
summary(gaussian_vario_ML)
summary(spherical_vario_ML)

plot(empirical_variog,
     type = "p",
     pch  = 19,
     xlab = "Distance (h)",
     ylab = expression(gamma(h)),
     ylim = range(c(empirical_variog$v, gamma_h)),
     main = "Empirical vs. Fitted Semivariograms"
     )

lines(exponential_vario_ML, col = "#E69F00")
lines(gaussian_vario_ML, col = "blue")
lines(spherical_vario_ML, col = "red")

legend("bottomright",
       legend = c("Empirical", "Exponential", "Gaussian", "Spherical"),
       col = c("black", "#E69F00", "blue", "red"),
       lty = c(NA, 1, 1, 1),
       lwd = c(NA, 1, 1, 1),
       pch = c(19, NA, NA, NA),
       bty = "n"
       )
```



# Kriging

Now that we have our variogram selected (spherical variogram with $\phi$ = 795.8 (range parameter), $\sigma^2$ = 0.118 (variance parameter, partial sill), nugget 0.102), we can proceed with kriging (i.e. forming a prediction surface for unobserved locations)

INLA will be used to fit a bayesian 


```{r}
meuse.grid.poly <- as(meuse.grid, "SpatialPolygons")
meuse.boundary <- surveillance::unionSpatialPolygons(meuse.grid.poly)
plot(meuse.boundary)

## adding a mesh over this region

# getting coords
boundary.pts <- meuse.boundary@polygons[[1]]@Polygons[[1]]@coords
mesh <- fmesher::fm_mesh_2d_inla(loc = meuse@coords,
                                 loc.domain = boundary.pts, 
                                 max.edge = c(150, 500), 
                                 offset = c(100, 250))
plot(mesh)
plot(meuse.boundary, add = TRUE, col = rgb(0, 0, 1, 0.25), lwd = 2)
points(meuse@coords, pch = 16, col = rgb(1,0,0,0.2), cex = 0.5)
```


```{r}
spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh)
# creating observation/prediction weight matrices for mesh models
A_matrix <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coordinates(meuse))

# making spatial field index vectors
s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field", n.spde = spde$n.spde)

## stacking all the information above together

# stack for fitting the model
stack.modelfit <- inla.stack(
  data = list(lead = meuse$lead),
  A = list(A_matrix, 1),
  effects = list(c(s.index, list(Intercept = 1)),
                 list(dist = meuse$dist)),
  tag = "data"
)

# prediction stack
A.pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = mesh, loc = coordinates(meuse.grid))
stack.pred <- inla.stack(
  data = list(lead = NA),
  A = list(A.pred, 1),
  effects = list(c(s.index, list(Intercept = 1)),
                 list(dist = meuse.grid$dist)),
  tag = "pred"
)

join.stack <- inla.stack(stack.modelfit, stack.pred)

inla.out.1 <- inla(
  formula = log(lead) ~ -1 + Intercept + dist + f(spatial.field, model = spde), #formula
  data = inla.stack.data(join.stack, spde = spde), # data and covariance model
  family = "gaussian",
  control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(join.stack), compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(cpo = TRUE, dic = TRUE)
)

summary(inla.out.1)

inla.out.1$summary.fixed
inla.out.1$summary.random
```
